source.filename: 2021-Experimental validation of the applicability of effective spring boundary conditions for modelling damaged interfaces in laminate structures.pdf

actuation: Piezoelectric actuation using thin circular PZT transducers (PZT PIC 151, 10 mm diameter, 0.5 mm thickness) to excite guided waves
constitutive_assumptions: All waveguide layers are composed of isotropic, linearly elastic materials obeying Hooke's law and Lamé elastodynamic equations
Time-harmonic wave motion with angular frequency omega
Stress-free traction boundary conditions at outer surfaces of the laminate waveguide
Continuity of traction vectors across internal layer interfaces
Imperfect interface modeled via effective spring boundary conditions (ESBC) with a diagonal spring stiffness matrix where normal and tangential stiffnesses are equal (kappa_11 = kappa_22 = kappa)
Quasi-static approximation for interface micro-cracks where defect width is much smaller than the wavelength (l << lambda)
Substrate layer of the retro-reflective tape assumed to be mechanically identical to the epoxy film
control_variables: Aluminium layer thickness (2 mm per plate)
Adhesive layer thickness (40 um two-sided epoxy tape)
Laminate curing duration and pressure (24 hours at room temperature under 1600 Pa uniform pressure)
Surface preparation cleaning procedure (degreasing with isopropanol prior to bonding)
Piezoelectric transducer dimensions and material (PZT PIC 151, 10 mm diameter, 0.5 mm thickness)
Laser Doppler vibrometer head distance (~1100 mm above the specimen)
Retro-reflective tape specifications (3M 7610 Scotchlite, 100 um thickness)
Damping treatment on specimen edges (plasticine application to suppress side-wall reflections)
dependent_variables: Out-of-plane surface velocity v(x1, zM, t) measured by laser Doppler vibrometry
Wavenumber and slowness spectrum W(f, s) of propagating guided waves obtained via 2D Fourier transform
Dispersion characteristics and slownesses of specific guided wave modes (GW1 to GW6)
Identified interfacial spring stiffness kappa (GPa/mm) and estimated damage parameter product Cl (mm)

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Effective spring boundary conditions (ESBC) expressing spring stiffness in terms of material moduli and micro-crack geometry can quantitatively and qualitatively model guided wave dispersion changes in multi-layered laminates with damaged interfaces.

Different guided wave modes show different sensitivity to interface degradation: even-numbered modes (GW2, GW4, GW6) exhibit significantly greater shifts in slowness with decreasing spring stiffness than odd-numbered modes (GW1, GW3, GW5).

For aluminium-epoxy laminates with mechanical surface scratches, ESBC stiffness was experimentally evaluated in the range 40-60 GPa/mm (Cl = 0.01-0.02 mm), matching manufacturing estimates (Cl = 0.005-0.015 mm).
For laminates with strip-like knife cuts at the interface, ESBC stiffness was experimentally identified between 2 and 4 GPa/mm (Cl = 0.25-0.5 mm), matching measured crack geometry (Cl = 0.1-0.4 mm).

Severe abrasive degradation of the adhesive film using emery led to spring stiffness kappa < 1 GPa/mm (Cl > 0.35 mm), causing guided wave slownesses to approach the behavior of a fully debonded interface.

experimental_setup: Three-layered laminate specimens consisting of two 2 mm-thick aluminium plates bonded with a 40 um-thick two-sided epoxy tape, cured for 24 h at room temperature under 1600 Pa pressure

Four interface conditions investigated: pristine/undamaged interface, lower epoxy surface partially abraded with emery, upper aluminium surface scratched with a wire brush, and upper aluminium surface notched with strip-like knife cuts (0.2-0.5 mm wide)
Circular piezoelectric actuators (PZT PIC 151, 10 mm diameter, 0.5 mm thick) adhesively mounted to excite elastodynamic guided waves
Polytec PSV-500-V laser Doppler vibrometer (LDV) positioned 1100 mm above the specimen scanning out-of-plane surface velocity along a central line
3M 7610 Scotchlite high gain retro-reflective sheeting strip (100 um thick) applied along the LDV scanning path to enhance signal-to-noise ratio
Plasticine applied around the specimen borders to minimize edge boundary reflections
future_work: Extending the ESBC methodology to account for other micro-defect geometries such as circular, elliptical, or rectangular cracks using alternative stiffness relations
Applying the modeling framework to more complex composite materials and anisotropic media
independent_variables: Type and severity of interfacial damage (intact/perfect contact, wire brush scratches, strip-like cuts, and emery-damaged adhesive)
Excitation wave frequency (evaluated in the range 0.1 MHz to 0.8 MHz)
Spatial position x1 along the specimen surface measurement line
limitations_inferred: The investigation is restricted to planar two-dimensional wave propagation and simple flat specimen geometries, not addressing complex 3D structures or curved components
Manual defect fabrication techniques (knife cutting, wire brush scratching, emery sanding) generate non-uniform crack geometry and spacing across the interface
The paper evaluates static manufactured damage in structural metals/epoxy laminates and does not investigate soft robotic materials, elastomers, or active variable-stiffness devices
limitations_stated_by_authors: Analytical expressions for spring stiffness (Eqs. 5 and 6) strictly apply only to planar arrays of strip-like micro-cracks oriented perpendicular to wave propagation and are not strictly valid for non-aligned random scratch patterns
The quasi-static approximation parameter zeta(f) is frequency-dependent in reality, decreasing by up to 50% as frequency increases
Different defect shapes (circular, elliptical) require distinct formulations for effective interfacial spring stiffnesses
The retro-reflective tape substrate was simplified as mechanically identical to the epoxy layer in the numerical waveguide model
main_results: Experimental validation demonstrated that ESBC accurately captures the changes in guided wave dispersion caused by imperfect and degraded laminate interfaces

Estimated interfacial spring stiffnesses matched theoretical calculations based on physical crack density and width measurements (scratched aluminium: kappa = 40-60 GPa/mm; strip cuts: kappa = 2-4 GPa/mm; abraded adhesive: kappa < 1 GPa/mm)
Guided wave mode GW2 was particularly sensitive to slight surface scratching, while GW3 shifted markedly toward debonded behavior under severe interface degradation
The contact degradation severity in multi-layer structures can be classified and quantitatively reconstructed through frequency-wavenumber analysis combined with ESBC
modeling_methods: Lamé elastodynamic differential formulation for in-plane wave propagation in multi-layered isotropic waveguides
Effective spring boundary conditions (ESBC) specifying stress traction continuity and displacement jump proportional to interfacial spring stiffness (tau = kappa * [u])
Spatial Fourier transform with respect to coordinate x1 to convert the governing partial differential equations into ordinary differential equations and establish linear dispersion algebraic systems
Quasi-static micromechanical modeling (Baik-Thompson and Lekesiz-Katsube-Rokhlin-Seghi models) relating spring stiffness to crack density, average defect width, and elastic constants
Two-dimensional Fourier transform frequency-wavenumber analysis (FWA) of measured surface velocity profiles to extract experimental dispersion curves
performance_metrics: Guided wave slowness s (us/m) as a function of frequency f (MHz)
Damage parameter product Cl (crack density C multiplied by average defect width l, mm)
Agreement/discrepancy between theoretical and experimental dispersion curves
possible_gap_implications: The ESBC framework could potentially provide a theoretical and experimental basis for modeling interfacial compliance or bond degradation between flexible composite layers or bonded soft-rigid interfaces

Guided wave inspection with ESBC could potentially be adapted for non-destructive health evaluation of laminated flexible components, though high material damping in soft elastomers remains an unexamined challenge
paper.research_objective: To experimentally validate theoretical estimations of interfacial spring stiffnesses in effective spring boundary conditions (ESBC) for modeling guided wave propagation in multi-layered laminates with damaged interfaces, and to demonstrate its utility for identifying and classifying interface degradation.
paper.research_problem: Accurate non-destructive evaluation and mechanical modeling of interfacial degradation and weakened adhesion in adhesively bonded multi-layered laminate structures using ultrasonic guided waves and effective spring boundary conditions.
paper.title: Experimental validation of the applicability of effective spring boundary conditions for modelling damaged interfaces in laminate structures
